newsitem.title: UK: British utility Eurobonds steady on tax plans.
newsitem.headline: British utility Eurobonds steady on tax plans.

text.p: Spreads on sterling Eurobonds issued by British utilities were stable on Wednesday, after the government announced windfall tax plans in line with expectations.
"We were expecting a windfall tax of up to five billion stg and that was where it came in," a Eurobond trader at a British bank said.
"It seems to cover all the companies we were expecting. It is early days, but I don't think there will be a big impact," he said.
Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown said in his budget speech he would raise a net 4.8 billion stg through a one-off tax on companies privatised by flotation and subject to economic regulation.
The so-called "windfall" tax would raise some 2.1 billion stg from the electricity sector, around 1.65 billion stg from water companies and 1.45 billion stg from others, he said.
The companies affected include BAA Plc, British Energy Plc, British Gas/Centrica, British Telecommunications Plc and electricity and water companies.

A trader at one British bank said he would mark utility bond spreads a couple of basis points tighter on Wednesday due to the "relief factor" that taxes were not higher than expected. Another trader said he would keep spreads unchanged.

The Inland Revenue said the tax would be charged at a rate of 23 percent on the difference between company value at the time of flotation and company value relative to profits over a period of up to four years following privatisation.
The tax will be payable in two instalments, the first on December 1, 1997 and the second a year later.
British utility companies are active borrowers in the sterling Eurobond market, and bankers said some could issue new bonds to fund their tax payments.
"Once companies start preparing further borrowing plans, spreads on their bonds could widen a bit," one dealer said.
Anglian Water Plc finance director said after the budget his company would have to borrow to pay the utility tax, which was likely to be around 170 million stg for his company.
